title: The Particle Model of Matter
summary: Use the particle model to explain the three states of matter, changes of state, diffusion, expansion and contraction, density and pressure.

notes.text: The **particle model of matter** is a scientific model that explains how matter behaves. It states that:

items: All matter is made of tiny particles (atoms or molecules).
There are empty spaces between the particles.
The particles are always moving. The higher the temperature, the faster they move.
There are forces of attraction between particles. The closer they are, the stronger the forces.

notes.caption: The three states of matter
rows: Closely packed in a regular pattern
Close together, but not in a pattern
Move around and slide past each other
Takes the shape of its container

notes.caption: Particle arrangement in a solid, a liquid and a gas

rows: Solid → gas directly (e.g. dry ice, iodine)

notes.text: When a solid is heated, its particles gain energy and vibrate faster. At the **melting point** they vibrate so much that they break free of their fixed positions. Pure water melts at **0 °C** and boils at **100 °C** at sea level. During a change of state the temperature stays constant, because the energy is used to overcome the forces between particles.
The spreading out of particles from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration, caused by their random movement.

Diffusion explains why you can smell perfume across a room, or why a drop of food colouring spreads through water. It is fastest in gases, slower in liquids, and happens faster at higher temperatures.

When a substance is heated, its particles move faster and further apart, so the substance **expands** (its volume increases). When it cools it **contracts**. The particles themselves do NOT get bigger.

items: Gaps are left between sections of railway lines and bridges so that they can expand on hot days.
A liquid-in-glass thermometer works because the liquid expands up the tube when heated.
A tight metal jar lid can be loosened by running hot water over it.

notes.caption: Density is measured in g/cm³ or kg/m³

notes.title: Calculating density
notes.problem: A block of wood has a mass of 120 g and a volume of 200 cm³. Calculate its density. Will it float on water (density 1 g/cm³)?
steps: 0,6 g/cm³ is less than 1 g/cm³, so the wood floats.

notes.text: Solids are usually the densest state, because their particles are packed most closely. **Gas pressure** is caused by gas particles colliding with the walls of their container. Heating a gas in a closed container increases the pressure, because the particles move faster and hit the walls more often and harder.

questions.prompt: In which state do particles only vibrate in fixed positions?
Which state of matter can be compressed easily?
questions.explanation: Gas particles have large spaces between them.

questions.prompt: What is the change of state from gas to liquid called?
What is the name for the spreading of particles from a high to a low concentration?
When a metal rod expands, its particles become bigger.
questions.explanation: The particles move further apart; they do not change size.

questions.prompt: A stone has a mass of 270 g and a volume of 100 cm³. Calculate its density.
Match each change of state to what happens.
Use the particle model to explain why gaps are left between sections of a railway line.
questions.memo:
✓ On hot days the particles in the steel gain energy and move/vibrate faster (1)
✓ They move further apart, so the steel expands (1)
✓ Without gaps the rails would push against each other and buckle (1)

questions.prompt: Explain why perfume sprayed in one corner of a room can soon be smelt in the opposite corner.
questions.memo:
✓ Perfume particles evaporate and move randomly through the air (1)
✓ They diffuse from where they are concentrated to where there are few of them (1)

questions.prompt: Why does the air pressure inside a closed bottle increase when the bottle is left in the hot sun?
questions.memo:
✓ The gas particles gain energy and move faster (1)
✓ so they collide with the walls more often and with more force (1)
